arXiv:2611.06803v1 [cs.AI] 04 Nov 2026

Task-efficient agent evaluation using cached traces

Ben Johnson Affiliation: Jataware    Hayden Helm ††thanks: Corresponding author: hayden@helivan.io Affiliation: Helivan
Abstract

Efficient benchmarking estimates a system’s full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family-, and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system’s score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon p<10−4p<10^{-4}) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon p<10−3p<10^{-3}), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Generative model use is increasingly agentic: systems plan, invoke tools, observe intermediate results, and iterate over long horizons to complete complex tasks (Yang et al., 2024; Wang and others, 2025). As agentic capabilities increase, so does the range of settings in which a given system might be deployed – and, with it, the number of benchmarks on which the system must be evaluated before it can be trusted with consequential work (Kapoor et al., 2026). Agentic evaluation, however, is expensive. Each task execution requires a properly sandboxed environment and routinely consumes hundreds of thousands of tokens (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026). Full evaluation on a benchmark can regularly exceed $2,000 (Kapoor et al., 2026). Given this cost, efficient evaluation is necessary to improve the evaluation coverage of an agentic system.

Task-efficient evaluation methods address this problem by finding structure in item-level information available from previously evaluated reference systems to mitigate the cost of evaluating a new system. Some task-efficient evaluation methods require only the item-level scores from reference systems (Maia Polo et al., 2024; Vivek et al., 2024; Kipnis et al., 2025; Bowyer et al., 2026). Others leverage information in cached artifacts, such as natural language responses (Acharyya et al., 2024; Helm et al., 2025) or residual streams (Duderstadt et al., 2023), to measure the similarity of systems on a set of tasks. Agentic workflows often produce artifacts when executing a task – file diffs, tool calls, intermediate plans, and error messages – recorded together in an execution trace that can be used to this effect. Existing methods for using cached artifacts rely on off-the-shelf embedding functions that typically capture system or model idiosyncrasies (Sun et al., 2025) better than trace functionality. Along these lines, we make two primary contributions:

  1. 1.

    trubric trace representations. We introduce trubric (trace rubric): a trace representation constructed by extracting a task-specific structured summary of a trace with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. We show that trubric embeddings preserve information relevant to the task and behavior of the system while minimizing system-, model family-, and harness-specific signal across seven modern text encoders.

  2. 2.

    Task-efficient evaluation using cached traces. Given the trubric embeddings from a set of tasks for a target system and a collection of reference systems, we evaluate their utility for predicting the target system’s full benchmark score on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 under three different agentic system evaluation protocols. We find that trubric-based estimators, combined with an item-response model, reduce single task mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (p<10−4p<10^{-4}) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (p<10−3p<10^{-3}) on the two benchmarks, respectively, and are nearly always better than baselines at every task budget (Table 1).

1.1 Problem statement

For our purposes, an agentic system f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} is a random mapping from a task space 𝒯\mathcal{T} to a trace space 𝒳\mathcal{X}. A benchmark is a fixed collection of tasks T∗={t1,…,tM}⊂𝒯T^{*}=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{M}\}\subset\mathcal{T}. Each trace is evaluated by the benchmark’s trace-level scoring function s:𝒳→{0,1}s:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} and the system has a benchmark score y⁡(f)=1M​∑j=1M𝔼⁡[s⁡(f⁡(tj))]y(f)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left[s(f(t_{j}))\right], where the expectation is with respect to the randomness of ff. We write yy for y⁡(f)y(f) and yiy_{i} for y⁡(fi)y(f_{i}) when the context is clear.

When evaluating a new system, we typically have access to 𝒟={{(xi​j,s⁡(xi​j))}j=1M}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\left\{\{(x_{ij},s(x_{ij}))\}_{j=1}^{M}\right\}_{i=1}^{n}, the traces and trace-level scores of nn previously evaluated reference systems f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n}, where xi​j∼fi​(tj)x_{ij}\sim f_{i}(t_{j}). For the target system f0f_{0}, we observe traces (and, optionally, trace-level scores) on only a subset T⊂T∗T\subset T^{*} with |T|=m≪M|T|=m\ll M tasks and our goal is to estimate the system’s full benchmark score y0y_{0} using only the target’s mm execution traces (and, optionally, their scores) and 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

2 Related work

Representing agentic traces.

The standard tools for embedding model artifacts are text encoders trained on sentence-level semantic similarity (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Su et al., 2023; Nussbaum and Duderstadt, 2025). Agentic traces, however, implicitly or explicitly encode system metadata that may not be relevant for downstream tasks (Sun et al., 2025; Oderinwale, 2026) and are therefore not necessarily encoded well by semantic embedding models. Instead, traces have primarily been studied through taxonomies of failure modes and actions (Cemri et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2026) and LLM judges (Zhuge et al., 2025; Mehtiyev and Assunção, 2026). Parallel work uses LLMs to adapt outputs to be more naturally compared via their semantics (Ravfogel et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024; Benara et al., 2024). trubric applies this to agentic traces by embedding a task-specific structured summary of each trace.

Efficient benchmarking.

Task-efficient benchmarking estimates a system’s full benchmark score from a small number of executions. The dominant paradigm for efficient benchmarking centers around item response theory (IRT) (Birnbaum, 1968), where a target system’s score is estimated with m≤Mm\leq M item-level scores by assigning a latent ability based on the relationship between a task’s difficulty and discriminability (Maia Polo et al., 2024; Kipnis et al., 2025). Extensions of IRT select informative or adaptive task subsets (Vivek et al., 2024; Truong et al., 2025). A complementary paradigm represents the systems themselves, either from their score profiles (Ruan et al., 2024; Zhuang et al., 2025) or from the artifacts they produce while executing a task (Duderstadt et al., 2023; Acharyya et al., 2024; Helm et al., 2025). For example, the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS) (Helm et al., 2026a) represents language models as Euclidean objects obtained via multidimensional scaling of the distances between their embedded responses. Helm et al. (2026b) regress benchmark scores on similar representations and prove that the estimate is task-efficient relative to the sample score. trubric enables extending geometry-based methods to agentic systems by providing an effective trace encoding. We show that these two approaches – score-based IRT and trace-based PKPS – can be combined to outperform either constituent for any given number of executed tasks when the full set of reference systems is available.

3 Methods

We first present trubric. We then describe constructing representations of the systems f0,f1,…,fnf_{0},f_{1},\ldots,f_{n} based on trubric embeddings that can be used to train a simple regressor in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for task-efficient evaluation. We evaluate the proposed methods in Section 4.

3.1 Task-specific rubrics for representing traces

A trace representation for benchmark prediction should place two traces close together when they reflect similar execution behavior on a task. Concretely, we consider five attributes of a trace that a representation might encode: (i) task (i.e., which task the trace corresponds to), (ii) correctness (i.e., whether the trace produced a correct output), (iii) system identity (i.e., which system produced the trace), (iv) model family (i.e., the family of the underlying generative model), and (v) harness (i.e., the harness used to produce the trace). For efficient benchmarking with traces, an ideal representation encodes (i) and (ii) but not (iii)–(v). trubric constructs such a representation in two stages.

First, for each task tjt_{j}, an LLM is prompted with the task description to instantiate a task-specific rubric. The rubric is a set of KK fields Rj=(rj(1),…,rj(K))R_{j}=(r_{j}^{(1)},\ldots,r_{j}^{(K)}) where each field describes an aspect of execution behavior (e.g., how the relevant code was found). Rubrics are shared across all traces for a given task and fields are shared across tasks. An example rubric is provided in Appendix A.1.

Second, for each trace xi​jx_{ij} we use an LLM to produce a short summary zi​j(k)z_{ij}^{(k)} for each field. The summary of each field is then embedded separately with a semantic embedding model gg mapping text to ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p} and concatenated to yield the trace representation ϕ⁡(xi​j)=(g⁡(zi​j(1)),…,g⁡(zi​j(K)))∈ℝK⋅p\phi(x_{ij})=(g(z_{ij}^{(1)}),\ldots,g(z_{ij}^{(K)}))\in\mathbb{R}^{K\cdot p}. Two examples of an extracted summary for a given task are provided in Appendix A.1.

Figure 1 compares trubric to two baselines along axes (i)–(v). Values closer to the edge correspond to a more ideal representation for efficient benchmarking for a given attribute. Experiment details are provided in Section 4.

3.2 Inference in the Product Kernel Perspective Space

Given trace representations, we represent agentic systems via the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS). Before constructing the geometry of systems, trace representations are centered by subtracting the average across systems for each task and field to emphasize differences in behavior. Let τ\tau denote a text embedding of the task description and κσ(t,t′)=exp(−∥τ(t)−τ(t′)∥2/2σ2)\kappa_{\sigma}(t,t^{\prime})=\exp\left(-\|\tau(t)-\tau(t^{\prime})\|^{2}/2\sigma^{2}\right). Let ⟨ϕ,ϕ′⟩=ϕT​ϕ′\langle\phi,\phi^{\prime}\rangle=\phi^{T}\phi^{\prime} for ϕ,ϕ′∈ℝK⋅p\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\cdot p}. For systems faf_{a} and fbf_{b} evaluated on task sets TaT_{a} and TbT_{b}, define the weighted similarity

⟨fa,fb⟩=∑t∈Ta∑t′∈Tbκσ​(t,t′)​⟨ϕ⁡(xa​t),ϕ⁡(xb​t′)⟩∑t∈Ta∑t′∈Tbκσ​(t,t′),\langle f_{a},f_{b}\rangle=\frac{\sum_{t\in T_{a}}\sum_{t^{\prime}\in T_{b}}\kappa_{\sigma}(t,t^{\prime})\,\langle\phi(x_{at}),\phi(x_{bt^{\prime}})\rangle}{\sum_{t\in T_{a}}\sum_{t^{\prime}\in T_{b}}\kappa_{\sigma}(t,t^{\prime})}, (1)

the corresponding squared distance δ2​(fa,fb)=⟨fa,fa⟩+⟨fb,fb⟩−2​⟨fa,fb⟩\delta^{2}(f_{a},f_{b})=\langle f_{a},f_{a}\rangle+\langle f_{b},f_{b}\rangle-2\langle f_{a},f_{b}\rangle, and Δa​b=δ2​(fa,fb)\Delta_{ab}=\delta^{2}(f_{a},f_{b}). With Δ\Delta defined on f0,f1,…,fnf_{0},f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}, applying classical multidimensional scaling (Torgerson, 1952) to Δ\Delta yields dd-dimensional Euclidean representations (ψ0,ψ1,…,ψn)∈ℝ(n+1)×d(\psi_{0},\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times d} of the systems with respect to the collective task sets. Importantly, Eq. (1) is defined when |Ta|≠|Tb||T_{a}|\neq|T_{b}| if both |Ta|>0|T_{a}|>0 and |Tb|>0|T_{b}|>0, so the target system is naturally represented in the same space as the reference systems. It is typical that |T0|=m≪M|T_{0}|=m\ll M and |Ti|=M|T_{i}|=M for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.

Given 𝒟\mathcal{D} and ψ1,…,ψn\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{n}, we train a simple regressor on (ψ1,y1),…,(ψn,yn)(\psi_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(\psi_{n},y_{n}) and apply it to ψ0\psi_{0} to obtain y^geom\hat{y}_{\mathrm{geom}}, an estimate of f0f_{0}’s full benchmark score y0y_{0}. Figure 2 shows the d=2d=2 perspectives when using the raw-trace embeddings (top) and the trubric embeddings (bottom) for different numbers of reference systems and numbers of executed tasks per system. Each dot is a system colored by its full benchmark score on SWE-bench Verified. The trubric-based PKPS contains more information, per a lower mean absolute error on leave-one-system-out evaluation (LOSO; see Section 4). Finally, we note that y^geom\hat{y}_{\mathrm{geom}} does not use any item-level score information.

4 Experiments

We next introduce the datasets we use to evaluate the trace embeddings and the trace-based geometries for efficient evaluation, describe the trace embedding analysis and three different agent evaluation protocols, and describe baselines. We then evaluate trubric-based estimators against baselines across benchmarks, evaluation protocols, task budgets, and design choices.

Benchmark data.

We consider two agentic benchmarks:

  1. 1.

    SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024) consists of 500 human-validated software-engineering tasks drawn from real GitHub issues. Its public leaderboard includes submissions from 119 unique systems. We consider the 107 systems with complete public trace archives and per-task outcomes. We downsampled to M=100M=100 tasks (Appendix C). We let yiy_{i} be the official resolve rate over all 500 tasks. The full list of systems and tasks is included in Appendix C.

  2. 2.

    Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) consists of 89 command-line tasks executed under a standardized harness specification. Its leaderboard contains submissions from 75 systems. Each system attempts each task five times. We analyze the 65 unique systems with at least 90% public trace coverage. We use a single trial’s trace and binary outcome for a given (system, task) and let yiy_{i} be the mean resolve rate across all tasks and all trials. The full list of systems and tasks is included in Appendix C.

Trace embedding evaluation.

To quantify what a trace representation encodes, we train balanced linear classifiers to predict each of the five attributes of Section 3.1 for a held-out trace from its embedding. Classifiers for the system-level attributes (iii)–(v) are evaluated on held-out tasks. Classifiers for (i) and (ii) are evaluated on held-out groups of systems. We evaluate trace representations using the cached SWE-bench Verified traces and report balanced accuracy for each attribute. Higher accuracy is preferred for attributes (i) and (ii). Near chance accuracy is preferred for attributes (iii)–(v). Detailed descriptions of the classification tasks are provided in Appendix A.2.

Trace embedding baselines.

We compare trubric embeddings to two baseline representations: raw trace, which uses gg to embed the start and end of each trace, and generic, which follows the two-stage construction of Section 3.1 with fixed field descriptions in place of a task-specific rubric. Unless otherwise stated, both the generic and trubric representations use K=6K=6 fields, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) as both the rubric generator and summarizer. For the embedding function gg, we consider seven text encoders: text-embedding-3-small (Neelakantan et al., 2022), nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (Nussbaum et al., 2025), bge-large-en-v1.5 (Xiao et al., 2024), gte-large (Li et al., 2023), e5-large-v2 (Wang et al., 2022), all-mpnet-base-v2, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). These encoders span open- and closed-source models, multiple architectures and training procedures, and embedding dimension sizes. The prompts and fixed field descriptions are provided in Appendix A.3.

Efficient benchmarking evaluation protocols.

Modern leaderboards contain many entries that share an underlying model or harness. To emulate the process of evaluating a new model or harness, as well as a new combination of the two, we consider three different evaluation protocols: leave-one-system-out where only the target itself is excluded from the references, leave-one-family-out where references whose underlying model family matches the target’s are additionally excluded, and leave-one-harness-out where references sharing the target’s harness are excluded. Detailed descriptions of a system’s assignment to a model family or harness are provided in Appendix C.

Efficient benchmarking baselines.

We compare trubric-based predictions against five baselines: the population mean (the mean benchmark score of the reference systems), the sample score (the mean of the target’s mm observed trace-level scores), raw trace (the PKPS pipeline applied to the raw-trace embeddings), generic (the PKPS pipeline applied to the generic rubric embeddings), and two-parameter IRT. We also consider the convex combination y^α=α​y^IRT+(1−α)​y^geom\hat{y}_{\alpha}=\alpha\,\hat{y}_{\mathrm{IRT}}+(1-\alpha)\,\hat{y}_{\mathrm{geom}}, with α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] selected via cross-validation. We refer to the convex combination as IRT ++ trubric. For trubric, raw trace, and generic, the regressor and its hyperparameters are selected per task draw via cross-validation on the reference systems. Implementation details for all estimators, including a technical description of IRT, are provided in Appendix B.

Task selection methods.

For each task budget mm, we consider two methods for selecting the target’s mm executed tasks. Random selection draws the mm tasks uniformly. Reported results average over 50 randomly sampled task subsets. Adaptive selection chooses tasks greedily using the fitted item-response model. In particular at each step, the task with the highest expected Fisher information under the current ability posterior is executed and the posterior is updated (Appendix B).

4.1 Results

Rubric-based preprocessing produces more useful trace representations.

Figure 1 shows that both generic and task-specific rubrics reduce recoverable information about system identity, model family, and harness while retaining task and correctness information. As discussed above, these attributes can introduce nuisance variation and obscure similarities in how systems execute tasks. Task-specific rubrics produce a larger reduction in identity-related signals compared to generic rubrics. These qualitative patterns persist across all seven embedding models.

The differences in attributes (i)–(v) are also reflected in the quality of the system-level geometry for predicting benchmark score. Figure 2 shows a stronger relationship between system position in the embedding space and benchmark score for trubric than for raw-trace embeddings. In Figure 3, leave-one-system-out prediction error decreases more rapidly with additional tasks when using trubric representations than when using raw-trace embeddings. On SWE-bench Verified under leave-one-family-out evaluation, increasing the task budget from 1 to 20 reduces geometry-only MAE from 0.081 to 0.060 for trubric, compared with 0.099 to 0.089 for raw traces. Table 1 further shows that generic rubrics are competitive on SWE-bench at small budgets, though task-specific rubrics provide larger improvements on Terminal-Bench 2.0. For the remainder of the paper “trace geometry” refers to a trubric-based geometry.

Trace geometry supports task-efficient benchmark prediction.

Table 1 and Figure 3 show that trubric-based geometry predicts full benchmark performance more accurately than the sample score for small task budgets (m≤10m\leq 10) and the population mean for all budgets. The trubric-based geometry can also outperform IRT, which exploits the correctness patterns of reference systems, at small task budgets. On SWE-bench, the geometry produces a more accurate estimate from 1 through 10 random tasks (Figure 3). On Terminal-Bench, y^geom\hat{y}_{\mathrm{geom}} outperforms IRT at one task, but y^IRT\hat{y}_{\mathrm{IRT}} is more accurate from three tasks onward. We emphasize that the geometric methods only require the target’s trace content, and not its correctness labels, which means that these methods are applicable in settings where grading target tasks is infeasible (e.g., due to cost, lack of expertise, etc.), provided scored reference systems are available. y^geom\hat{y}_{\mathrm{geom}} can be interpreted as a high-bias, low-variance estimate of the full benchmark score.

Combining trace geometry with IRT is best.

The trace-based predictions and correctness-based predictions exhibit different behavior as the task budget grows: trace-based predictions are informative with very few executions, while IRT improves substantially as the number of tasks increases. Figure 3 shows that combining their predictions improves prediction across all evaluated budgets and benchmarks. At m=5m=5 on SWE-bench, IRT ++ trubric achieves 0.063 MAE, compared with 0.069 for geometry alone (Wilcoxon’s p<10−4p<10^{-4}) and 0.088 for IRT (Wilcoxon’s p<10−12p<10^{-12}). On Terminal-Bench – where IRT is relatively stronger – the combination achieves 0.090, compared with 0.107 for geometry (Wilcoxon’s p<10−3p<10^{-3}) and 0.097 for IRT (Wilcoxon’s p<10−2p<10^{-2}). These results suggest a complementary predictive value of execution artifacts and correctness outcomes. The broad pattern persists across the system-, family-, and harness-exclusion protocols in Figure 3, although the size of the improvement varies.

Performance improves with larger reference sets.

The left panel of Figure 4 shows that increasing the number of reference systems generally improves both IRT and geometry-based estimators. At m=5m=5 random tasks on SWE-bench, expanding from n=20n=20 to n=107n=107 reduces geometry-only MAE from 0.086 to 0.069 and IRT ++ trubric MAE from 0.081 to 0.063. The contribution of geometry depends on reference availability: given a small number of reference systems and a large task budget, IRT can outperform geometry-only methods. The medium budget (m=20m=20), small-reference-set (n=20n=20) regime is the one setting where IRT outperforms the convex combination.

Adaptive task selection composes with trace-based estimation.

Adaptive task selection provides a further improvement. With m=5m=5 adaptive tasks, IRT ++ trubric achieves 0.048 MAE on SWE-bench, compared with 0.063 for five random tasks (Table 1). Together, Table 1 and the center panel of Figure 4 show that adaptive selection improves both IRT and geometry-based prediction and can further improve evaluation efficiency.

Prediction is insensitive to the choice of text encoder.

We evaluate the sensitivity of trubric-based prediction on SWE-bench to the choice of text encoder in the right panel of Figure 4. The effect is small (at most 0.008 MAE at any fixed setting) relative to the effect of the number of target tasks or task selection (0.081 to 0.060 from 1 to 20 random tasks; 0.063 to 0.048 for random versus adaptive selection at m=5m=5) and the number of reference systems (0.086 to 0.069 at m=5m=5).

The trace geometry reduces the cost of reaching a given prediction error.

Figure 5 translates the error curves into the cost of evaluating a system. For this comparison, we assume a cost of $2 per agent execution (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; Kapoor et al., 2026) and assume both the cost of using LLMs to do (t)rubric creation and summarization and the cost of embedding the traces are negligible. On SWE-bench, IRT ++ trubric reaches an MAE below 0.10 with one random task, compared with five tasks for IRT and twenty for the sample score. This corresponds to estimated target execution costs of $2, $10, and $40, respectively.

We also evaluate methods for comparing two systems head to head. For each pair of systems whose true benchmark scores differ by at least 0.05, we exclude both systems from the references and ask whether an estimator correctly identifies the better system from mm random executions per system (right two panels of Figure 5). On SWE-bench, IRT ++ trubric decides 88% of pairs correctly from a single task per system, compared with 79% for IRT and 69% for the sample score. By five tasks per system, all estimators exceed 90% and the score-based estimators are competitive or better. On Terminal-Bench, IRT is the most accurate estimator at every tested budget. Trace information is thus most valuable for head-to-head comparisons in the lowest budget regime, where executing a single task per system ($4 for the pair) identifies the better system in nearly nine of ten pairs.

Larger rubrics improve average performance.

Figure 6 varies the number of fields included in generic and task-specific rubrics, averaging performance over subsets drawn from a bank of 32 fields. For both constructions, adding fields generally improves average prediction accuracy. At m=5m=5 and a large set of reference systems, increasing a task-specific rubric from one to six fields reduces average MAE from 0.090 to 0.081 (Wilcoxon’s p<10−5p<10^{-5}). Using all 32 fields reduces it further to 0.077 (Wilcoxon’s p<10−3p<10^{-3}). Task-specific rubrics generally outperform generic rubrics, especially with fewer reference systems and larger number of executed tasks.

Figure 6 also reports the best performing rubric. Each point selects the lowest average error among the tested subsets separately for that setting. These post hoc selections demonstrate the existence of favorable small rubrics, which may be preferred in settings where embeddings of the traces are stored for long periods. Importantly, the selected subsets need not be nested as field count increases, so their performance need not improve monotonically. We did not attempt to optimize the fields. The full list of the 32 field names is provided in Appendix A.4.

5 Discussion

We introduced trubric, a trace representation constructed by extracting a task-specific structured summary of a trace with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. Across seven text encoders, trubric embeddings preserve information about the task and the correctness of an execution while minimizing idiosyncratic information about the system, model family, and harness that produced it.

We then proposed using trubric embeddings to induce representations of agentic systems for task-efficient evaluation. The resulting geometry supports accurate benchmark score prediction from as little as a single executed task and, combined with an item-response model, is never worse than either constituent at any task budget when the full set of reference systems is available.

The combined estimator reduces the cost of reaching an MAE below 0.10 on SWE-bench Verified from $10–$40 to $2 per system. These results are relatively robust to the major design choices: the text encoder, the number of rubric fields, and the task selection method. Importantly, these results support the claim that extracting more than binary correctness from cached executions can improve the efficiency of agentic evaluation as the number of systems and benchmarks continues to grow – providing a route toward improved evaluation coverage for a given system.

5.1 Limitations

We evaluated trubric along the five attributes relevant to efficient evaluation. We make no claims about the usefulness of the representation for other tasks one might consider with traces, such as change detection (Bridgeford and Helm, 2025), online monitoring (Helm et al., 2026c), early stopping (Ruan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), or steering (Rahn et al., 2024). We leave the study of trubric-like representations for these tasks to future work.

As mentioned above, we did not attempt to optimize the rubric. The rubric size experiment of Section 4.1 demonstrates that favorable small rubrics exist. Developing validated procedures for selecting or learning rubric fields, such as parameterizing meta-instructions, is an open problem that we expect to have a small to medium effect on accuracy. We also note that trubric’s fields can be reconfigured to amplify or dampen arbitrary dimensions of variation in the input data.

In our analysis we only consider DeepSeek-V4-Flash (accessed via OpenRouter) as the rubric generator and trace summarizer. We had intended to add other frontier models as part of our ablation study, but a provider’s API service banned our account and accused us of attempting to distill reasoning traces. We include this note as a warning: summarizing traces at the scale required for trace-based evaluation can resemble distillation to automated enforcement systems and may result in account bans. In any case, we leave the sensitivity analysis of the two roles to future work.

Finally, we only consider highly curated, paired settings where every reference system has executed (nearly) every task of a single benchmark. We do not consider references with sparse or disjoint task coverage, nor signal shared across benchmarks. The PKPS formulation we use throughout supports both – Eq. (1) is defined for unpaired task sets – and we expect less curated, larger reference collections to further reduce evaluation cost.

Appendix A Trace representation details

A.1 Example task, trace, rubrics, and extractions

We illustrate the trubric pipeline on SWE-bench Verified instance django__django-11099.

Task.

The problem statement, as provided to the rubric-instantiation LLM:

UsernameValidator allows trailing newline in usernames
Description

ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator use the regex
r’^[\w.@+-]+$’
The intent is to only allow alphanumeric characters as well as ., @, +, and -. However, a little known quirk of Python regexes is that $ will also match a trailing newline. Therefore, the user name validators will accept usernames which end with a newline. You can avoid this behavior by instead using \A and \Z to terminate regexes. For example, the validator regex could be changed to
r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’
in order to reject usernames that end with a newline.
I am not sure how to officially post a patch, but the required change is trivial - using the regex above in the two validators in contrib.auth.validators.

Instantiated trubric.

The six task-specific field descriptions generated for this instance:

understanding

Look for the agent to identify that the issue lies in the regex anchoring with $ in ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator, specifically that $ matches a trailing newline in Python, and that changing to \A and \Z is the proposed fix in django/contrib/auth/validators.py.

localization

Check that the agent correctly locates the two validator classes (ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator) in django/contrib/auth/validators.py and references the existing regex r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ in both.

reproduction

Look for the agent to write or run a test that confirms a username ending with a newline (e.g., ’validuser\n’) is currently accepted by the validators, possibly by using Django’s validate_username or directly instantiating the validators.

editing

Verify that the agent modifies the regex pattern in both validator classes from r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ to r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’, ensuring no other changes are made to the file.

verification

The agent should run the relevant test suite (e.g., tests/auth_tests/test_validators.py or full Django auth tests) to confirm that usernames with trailing newlines are now rejected, and that existing valid usernames still pass.

final state

The final state should show django/contrib/auth/validators.py with both regex patterns updated, and no other unintended modifications, with tests confirming the newline rejection behavior.

Generic rubric.

For contrast, the generic baseline uses the same six fields with fixed, task-agnostic descriptions shared by every task:

understanding

how the agent oriented itself before acting

localization

how it searched/navigated to find the relevant code

reproduction

whether/how it reproduced the issue before fixing

editing

what it changed (files, nature and size of the edit)

verification

whether it re-ran tests or a repro script after editing, and the OBSERVED outcome (passing/failing/errors)

final state

how the run ended (clean finish, step/cost limit, submitted unverified)

Extractions.

Structured summaries of two systems’ traces on this task, produced against the rubric above. The summaries describe execution behavior without reference to the harness or underlying model that produced the trace.

System A.
understanding

The agent identified that the issue stems from Python’s regex behavior where $ matches a trailing newline, and that changing the anchors to \A and \Z in both validators would fix it. It explicitly mentioned this during the initial inspection of the validator file.

localization

The agent searched for validators.py, found django/contrib/auth/validators.py, opened it, and located both ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator classes. It acknowledged the existing regex pattern r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ in both classes before making changes.

reproduction

The agent attempted to reproduce the bug by creating test_validators.py and simple_test_validators.py, but these scripts failed due to missing Django settings configuration. It then created regex_test.py to directly test the regex patterns, which ran successfully and confirmed rejection of a trailing newline after the fix, though it did not demonstrate acceptance before the fix.

editing

The agent edited lines 10 and 20 in django/contrib/auth/validators.py, changing the regex from r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ to r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’ in both ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator. The diff shows only these two regex changes to the file, with no other modifications.

verification

The agent ran the custom regex_test.py script, which output that both ASCII and Unicode validators rejected a username ending with a newline. It did not run the existing Django test suite (e.g., tests/auth_tests/test_validators.py) to verify the fix against formal tests.

final state

The final state includes django/contrib/auth/validators.py with both regex patterns updated to r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’. Three new files (test_validators.py, simple_test_validators.py, regex_test.py) were created, but no other existing files were modified. The agent submitted these changes.

System B.
understanding

The agent identified that the issue stems from Python’s regex behavior where $ matches a trailing newline, causing ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator to incorrectly accept usernames ending with newlines. It understood that replacing ^ and $ with \A and \Z would fix the anchoring issue, as described in the issue for django/contrib/auth/validators.py.

localization

The agent located the two validator classes, ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator, in django/contrib/auth/validators.py. It confirmed both classes use the existing regex pattern r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ and identified these as the exact locations requiring modification.

reproduction

The agent verified the issue by running a quick test comparing the old and new regex patterns against usernames with and without trailing newlines. The test confirmed that the old pattern matched usernames ending with a newline, while the new pattern correctly rejected them, and valid usernames still passed.

editing

The agent modified the regex pattern in both validator classes from r’^[\w.@+-]+$’ to r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’ in django/contrib/auth/validators.py. The diff shows only these two regex changes, with no other modifications made to the file.

verification

The agent ran the auth test suite which passed all 494 tests, including the tests in auth_tests/test_validators.py for UsernameValidatorsTests. It also ran a targeted test confirming that usernames with trailing newlines are now rejected by both validators while valid usernames still pass.

final state

The final state shows django/contrib/auth/validators.py with both regex patterns updated to r’\A[\w.@+-]+\Z’ in ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator. No other files were modified, and tests confirm the newline rejection behavior works correctly.

A.2 Linear classification tasks

For each combination of text encoder and trace representation, we assemble one embedding per trace for the executions of the 107 SWE-bench Verified systems on a fixed panel of 20 tasks (2,129 traces; a small number of executions are missing from the public archive). Rubric-based representations are the concatenated per-field embeddings of Section 3.1; raw-trace representations embed head and tail slices of the rendered log as two blocks. Each block is ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized and blocks are weighted equally.

Probes are linear classifiers trained with class-balanced squared loss and a ridge penalty; the penalty is selected along a closed-form regularization path using grouped cross-validation within the training folds. Evaluation is five-fold grouped cross-validation with seeded, size-balanced group allocation: for the system-level attributes (iii)–(v) the groups are tasks, so probes are evaluated on tasks unseen during training, and for (i)–(ii) the groups are model families, so probes are evaluated on systems from families unseen during training. We report balanced accuracy averaged over folds; chance balanced accuracy for a CC-class attribute is 1/C1/C. Figure 1 plots (accuracy−chance)/(1−chance)(\mathrm{accuracy}-\mathrm{chance})/(1-\mathrm{chance}) for attributes (i)–(ii) and its complement for (iii)–(v), so that better-for-evaluation is always outward. Table 2 reports the balanced accuracies underlying Figure 1.

The rubric-instantiation prompt ({problem} is the task description):

Here is a repository issue that a software-engineering agent will be asked to fix:

{problem}

Write an instance-specific rubric for judging an agent’s trace on THIS issue:
for each section below, one sentence saying what specifically to look for in
this instance (name the likely relevant modules/files/tests if inferable).

Sections: understanding, localization, reproduction, editing,
verification, final_state.
Respond with ONLY a JSON object with those keys, each a one-sentence string.

The extraction prompt ({rubric} is the instantiated trubric for the task, or the fixed generic rubric below for the generic baseline; {keys} the field names; the rendered trace is appended after the prompt):

Below is the (truncated) execution trace of a software-engineering agent.
Extract a factual description of the agent’s behavior for EACH of the following
sections. 30-60 words per section. Describe behavior only -- do not restate the
problem. If a section did not occur, write exactly what is missing (e.g. "never
ran any test after editing").

{rubric}

Respond with ONLY a JSON object with keys {keys}, each a string.

The generic rubric:

- understanding: how the agent oriented itself before acting
- localization: how it searched/navigated to find the relevant code
- reproduction: whether/how it reproduced the issue before fixing
- editing: what it changed (files, nature and size of the edit)
- verification: whether it re-ran tests or a repro script after editing,
  and the OBSERVED outcome (passing/failing/errors)
- final_state: how the run ended (clean finish, step/cost limit,
  submitted unverified)

A.4 Rubric field list

The rubric-size experiment of Figure 6 draws field subsets from a bank of 32 fields. The bank consists of the six canonical fields used throughout the paper – understanding, localization, reproduction, editing, verification, and final state – together with 26 additional fields: requirements, causal diagnosis, code context, planning, test design, edge cases, regression scope, feedback response, tool recovery, patch review, exploration breadth, hypothesis testing, search strategy, dependency handling, error interpretation, incrementalism, backtracking, code reuse, instruction adherence, efficiency, state tracking, assumption checking, output quality, risk management, domain knowledge, and completion confidence.

Appendix B Efficient benchmarking details

B.1 Score-only baselines

Sample score.

The mean of the target’s mm observed trace-level scores, y^sample=1m​∑t∈T0s⁡(f0​(t))\hat{y}_{\mathrm{sample}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{t\in T_{0}}s(f_{0}(t)).

Population mean.

The mean benchmark score of the reference systems, y^pop=1n​∑i=1nyi\hat{y}_{\mathrm{pop}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}, which ignores the target’s executions entirely.

Item-response model.

We fit the two-parameter logistic model ℙ⁡(s⁡(xi​j)=1)=sigmoid⁡(aj​(θi−bj))\mathbb{P}(s(x_{ij})=1)=\mathrm{sigmoid}\left(a_{j}(\theta_{i}-b_{j})\right) to the reference score matrix by maximum a posteriori estimation, with standard normal priors on the abilities θi\theta_{i} and difficulties bjb_{j} and a 𝒩⁡(0,1/10)\mathcal{N}(0,1/10) prior on the log-discriminations log⁡aj\log a_{j} (centering the slopes at the Rasch value of one), optimized with L-BFGS. Because the benchmark score aggregates tasks beyond the MM-task panel (all 500 tasks for SWE-bench Verified; all tasks and trials for Terminal-Bench 2.0), we additionally fit a monotone link from ability to benchmark score, y≈sigmoid⁡(c1​θ+c0)y\approx\mathrm{sigmoid}(c_{1}\theta+c_{0}), by least squares on the reference systems. For a target, we form a posterior over ability on a dense grid – the prior is a normal with the mean and standard deviation of the reference abilities – update it with the likelihood of the target’s mm observed trace-level scores, and report the posterior mean of the fitted ability-to-score link as y^IRT\hat{y}_{\mathrm{IRT}}.

Adaptive task selection.

Given the fitted item-response model, tasks are selected greedily per target: at each step, the next task is the one with the highest expected Fisher information aj2​pj​(θ)​(1−pj​(θ))a_{j}^{2}\,p_{j}(\theta)(1-p_{j}(\theta)) under the current ability posterior, the outcome is observed, and the posterior is updated. Random task selection instead draws T0T_{0} uniformly; reported random-selection results average over 50 shared draws.

B.2 Trace-geometry baselines

The raw-trace and generic-rubric estimators replace the trubric representation ϕ\phi in the pipeline of Section 3.2 and are otherwise identical. The raw-trace representation embeds the first and last portions of the rendered execution log as two blocks with the same encoder gg; representations are centered by the task-level median across systems and ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized. The generic-rubric representation follows the two-stage construction of Section 3.1 with the fixed field descriptions of Appendix A.3 in place of task-specific rubrics.

B.3 Hyperparameters and cross-validation

For each task draw, hyperparameters are selected by treating each reference system as a pseudo-target: its score is predicted from the remaining references (leave-one-out via the hat matrix for the ridge regressor), and the configuration minimizing the mean reference error is selected. The candidate grids are the kernel bandwidth σ2∈{med/2k}k=08\sigma^{2}\in\{\mathrm{med}/2^{k}\}_{k=0}^{8} where med\mathrm{med} is the median squared distance between task embeddings, the dimension d∈{8,16}d\in\{8,16\}, and the ridge penalty ∈{0.1,1.0}\in\{0.1,1.0\}. The ensemble weight α\alpha is selected on a 101101-point grid over [0,1][0,1] by the same reference-pseudo-target procedure.

Appendix C Systems and tasks
